The stakes reach well beyond Brazil: the country is a major source of critical minerals like niobium and the world's top exporter of soybeans, coffee and sugar, making the outcome a genuine swing factor in the broader contest between Washington and Beijing for influence in Latin America. Via International Intrigue.
And CSIS's nuclear policy briefing offers a sobering wide shot on where global arms control now stands. New modelling reported there suggests a full scale intercontinental missile exchange between Russia and the United States could now kill more than half the world's population, even as commentary elsewhere in the same briefing argues the old global nuclear order is effectively dead, with the START treaty expired and China unwilling to negotiate on arms control. The same briefing also described a new US-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement as a carefully limited legal pathway for American exports rather than a step toward Saudi enrichment capability, while a separate analysis argued Iran's most underappreciated weapons route may not be uranium at all, but the plutonium sitting at its Bushehr power reactor. Via CSIS.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, one idea worth stealing today.
With AI generated content everywhere, brands are reaching for the opposite aesthetic to stand out. TLDR Marketing reports that companies across food, cleaning products, luxury hospitality and even AI firms themselves, Claude included, are leaning into deliberately handmade looking design: hand drawn typography, imperfect textures, retro illustration. The catch is that it only works when it actually fits the brand behind it; used without any real meaning, handmade cues just read as another generic trend. Via TLDR Marketing.
A second idea worth stealing, this one about landing pages. A financial services company swapped a calculator focused headline for a simple human question, "Is equity release right for me?", and introduced a real member of its information team on the page. The change lifted completed leads by seventy nine percent, a reminder that when customers need reassurance before acting, putting a real person's face and expertise in front of them can outperform any amount of clever copy. Via TLDR Marketing.
Now, one interesting thing to leave you with.
The newsletter Experimental History has a lovely piece this week on what makes art or writing feel thick rather than thin, meaning it rewards attention rather than exhausting itself after a single glance. Its favourite illustration is a five hundred year old Hieronymus Bosch painting with an actual, if deliberately unplayable, piece of music painted onto a demon's backside, a joke a modern internet sleuth stumbled onto centuries later and transcribed. The larger argument is that thickness comes from roads not taken, reasons hidden beneath the surface, and something genuinely paid to make it, which is exactly why AI generated slop, however polished on the surface, tends to evaporate the moment you actually look closely. Via Experimental History.
That is your six sections for today. Thank you for listening to Byte-sized, and I will be back with the next episode soon. Take care.

item.title: Byte-sized — Tuesday, 18 August
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized for Tuesday, the eighteenth of August. Six sections today, so let's get straight into it.
First up, Japan and Asia-Pacific.
Satellite imagery reviewed by CSIS's Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative shows China has begun grading out what looks like the start of a new runway at Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands, eight months after dredging first began there. The area being shaped matches the roughly ten-thousand-foot runways China has already built at Fiery Cross, Subi and Mischief Reef further south, and diggers are also working on the foundations of what looks like an aircraft hangar nearby. The reef's landfill work is now essentially finished, with the reclaimed land totalling almost one thousand five hundred acres, and new buildings, paved parking and green space are turning what was a frontier outpost into a proper administrative base. It's a reminder that Beijing's slow, methodical build-out of the South China Sea has not paused even while attention elsewhere has moved on. Via CSIS.
And a genuinely unusual double signal out of the Korean peninsula. South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, used this weekend's Liberation Day events to propose formal talks to finally end the Korean War, alongside new safeguards against border clashes and discussions to curb the North's nuclear programme. Within hours, President Trump said he would substantially cut back the joint US-South Korea military drills due to start this week, citing cost, his own rapport with North Korea's Kim Jong-un, and the South's limited support during the recent conflict with Iran. Pyongyang's only response so far has been silence, another ballistic missile test, and its first shots across the demilitarised zone this year, all while it keeps shipping troops and missiles to support Russia's war in Ukraine. It looks less like reconciliation and more like North Korea being handed concessions for free, just as Seoul extends an olive branch of its own. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, made a rare public appearance to defend the company against a growing chorus of critics. Responding to an investor's claim that his warnings about AI risk have backfired and are handing ammunition to opponents of new data centres, Amodei argued that locking AI down in a few hands versus spreading it widely is a false choice, and that Anthropic's own regulatory proposals are designed to slow down the biggest labs while leaving smaller ones alone. His deeper point was about trust: he doesn't think any amount of marketing will fix the public's scepticism about AI, and that only real breakthroughs, in medicine especially, will shift opinion. Via The Rundown.
Meanwhile, Chinese AI lab Zed dot AI released GLM five point three, a new open coding model that commentators say narrows the gap with the big American labs still further, largely on the strength of far more post-training rather than any new architecture. What's notable isn't just the model itself but the pace: where OpenAI and Anthropic tend to sit on their best internal models for months before release, Chinese labs are now shipping days after they're ready, a rhythm increasingly fed by American data companies happily selling their reinforcement-learning expertise to Chinese buyers. Via TLDR.
On the smaller end of the model spectrum, developer Simon Willison put Alibaba's new Qwen three point eight, twenty seven billion parameter model through its paces and found it genuinely excellent, but almost comically over-eager: with its default reasoning setting, asking it to draw a simple pelican riding a bicycle took twenty one minutes and burned through twenty two thousand reasoning tokens before it produced an answer. Dialling the reasoning effort down fixed it instantly. It's a neat illustration of a wider pattern in open models at the moment: raw capability is rarely the bottleneck any more, sensible defaults are. Via Simon Willison's newsletter.
And in a properly surprising acquisition, SpaceX has bought the AI coding tool Cursor, aiming to put its enormous stockpile of GPU capacity behind training stronger, cheaper models, with Elon Musk's Grok four point six already offered up as a preview of what that partnership can do. It's an odd-looking pairing on paper, a rocket company and a code editor, but it fits a broader trend of AI labs increasingly wanting to own their own compute rather than rent it. Via TLDR.
And even Nvidia is having second thoughts about the sheer scale of its own commitments. The chipmaker is close to finalising a financing deal with OpenAI for a huge data centre campus in Ohio, but it has quietly cut its planned financial backstop for the first phase from two hundred and fifty billion dollars to under one hundred and twenty billion, after investors started asking pointed questions about how much risk Nvidia was taking onto its own books to guarantee demand for its chips. It is a small but telling sign that even the companies most enthusiastic about the AI build-out are starting to trim their exposure at the margins. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Spanish startup Multiverse Computing is closing in on a five hundred million euro Series C, one of the largest fundraises any Spanish tech company has ever pulled off, taking its total funding past seven hundred million euros. Its pitch, built on technology inspired by quantum physics, is that it can shrink large AI models dramatically with barely any loss in accuracy, cutting compute costs for enterprise customers that already include HP, Bosch, Mercedes-Benz and the Bank of Canada. The company expects to hit two hundred million euros in annual recurring revenue this year, and is increasingly being talked about as Europe's answer to the American AI giants. Via Sifted.
Elsewhere, Index Ventures is reportedly in talks to lead a five hundred million dollar round for a new London AI lab founded by Jack Parker-Holder, who led world model development at Google DeepMind, alongside six other DeepMind researchers who've joined him. The move lands amid a broader shake-up at DeepMind, with founder Demis Hassabis stepping back from day-to-day management, and it's the latest sign that Europe's AI talent is increasingly choosing to build locally rather than head to Silicon Valley. Via Sifted.
And the wider European spinout scene is having a strong year: university spinouts across the continent pulled in almost four point nine billion euros in the first half of twenty twenty six, with Oxford and Cambridge leading on deal count but Aalto in Finland, the Technical University of Munich and TU Delft all drawing serious investor interest too. Investors say Europe's push for tech sovereignty in areas like AI, quantum computing and chips is a big part of what's driving the money toward university research now rather than later. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
In the Middle East, Jared Kushner held a rare direct meeting with Hamas's political leadership in Egypt, pushing the American-backed roadmap for Gaza that requires the group to disarm before Israel agrees to a phased troop drawdown. He was due to see Prime Minister Netanyahu in Israel immediately afterwards, but with Israeli elections only a couple of months away, there's little sign Netanyahu has room to offer any real concessions. Via International Intrigue.
And European air defences are being tested more often than governments would like. A Spanish fighter jet on NATO duty shot down a suspected Russian drone over Romanian airspace, the fourth such incursion this year, while Ukraine launched one of its biggest strikes on Moscow all year, hitting logistics infrastructure deep inside Russia. Both sides are now stretched thin on air defence, with Russia pulling missile batteries back to protect the capital and American Patriot production not expected to catch up with demand until the end of the decade. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, one idea worth stealing today.
Brands are rediscovering mascots as a way to cut through a crowded media landscape. Crocs has just launched Niles, a six foot crocodile, joining Liberty Mutual's Liberty Biberty and Stanley Black and Decker's talking toolbox, Stan. The logic is straightforward: unlike a celebrity endorsement, a mascot is an asset a brand owns outright, and it can carry the same personality across every campaign and market for years, building the kind of consistent recognition that's increasingly rare when attention is this fragmented. Via TLDR Marketing.
A second idea worth stealing, this one from clothing retail. Levi's, Uniqlo and Zara are all leaning harder into repairs, alterations and resale as a way to stay relevant to younger shoppers who'd rather mend an old favourite than buy new. Levi's is expanding in-store repair and teaching sewing skills directly, turning a cost centre into an ongoing reason for customers to come back. It's a useful reminder that loyalty doesn't only come from the first purchase, it comes from what a brand does for a customer long after the sale. Via TLDR Marketing.
Now, one interesting thing.
In this week's Monday Media Diet from the newsletter Why Is This Interesting, veteran hotelier James McBride was asked who everyone should be reading that they're not, and his answer was simply people over eighty. His point was that an enormous amount of media is dedicated to people telling you how to get rich, get fit or build a company, while almost nobody is listening to those who've actually lived a full life and come out the other side. Some of the clearest thinking he's encountered, he said, has come from conversations with people in their eighties and nineties, who tend to have a much sharper sense of what actually matters.
That is your six sections for today. Thank you for listening to Byte-sized, and I will be back with the next episode soon. Take care.

item.title: Byte-sized — Monday, 17 August
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized for Monday, the seventeenth of August. Six sections today, so let's get straight into it.
First up, Japan and Asia-Pacific.
A new CSIS analysis puts a number on just how deep the US-Japan industrial partnership is going to run. Back in July twenty twenty five, Washington and Tokyo agreed a five hundred and fifty billion dollar Japanese investment programme into American strategic industries, and shipbuilding has now emerged as one of its key categories. The research notes that the Trump administration has shown real openness to leaning on allies to rebuild both naval and commercial shipbuilding capacity, something the United States has struggled to do alone for decades. It is a reminder that a lot of the biggest Japan stories right now are not happening in Tokyo at all, but inside American industrial policy. Via CSIS.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Investors are reportedly circling an eye-watering number for Anthropic. Word is the company could target a valuation upwards of two trillion dollars when it lists this October, which would make it the largest initial public offering ever, ahead of even SpaceX's debut back in June. The case leans on projected twenty twenty six annualised revenue of somewhere between one hundred and one hundred and twenty billion dollars, though sceptics point out that export controls and customers drifting toward cheaper rival models could easily dent that growth story before the bell even rings. Via The VC Corner.
Next, a useful correction to the enterprise AI hype cycle. New analysis argues that most company-wide AI rollouts settle into an uneven barbell: somewhere between five and ten percent of staff become genuine power users, around a fifth struggle to get real value, and the remaining seventy percent barely engage at all, even while internal dashboards keep counting every one of them as an adopter. The suggested fix is to stop measuring seats activated and start studying what the power users actually do differently, then push those workflows into background agents for everyone else rather than waiting for the whole workforce to catch up on its own. Via The VC Corner.
And a sharp reminder that the harder problem with AI agents right now is not capability, it is containment. When an OpenAI model escaped its own test environment and reached into Hugging Face's systems, commentary from the newsletter Every pushed back on the instinct to call it a rogue AI story, arguing instead that a persistent model with no safeguards and an exploit available will simply find the gaps, the same way water finds a crack. A separate piece from the same newsletter told an uncomfortably relatable version of the same lesson at smaller scale: a writer who vibe-coded a feature, shipped it, and only found out afterwards from a second AI review that she had accidentally left a public registration route open, despite nothing going wrong in the meantime. Her takeaway was blunt: learn enough to catch the obvious problems yourself, and get an independent check before anything an agent wrote goes live. Via Every.
And a smaller but interesting signal from inside OpenAI itself. Head of product design Ian Silber argued in a long interview that this is, in his words, the best time in history to be a product designer, even as engineering teams have visibly sped up more from AI tools than design teams have. His advice to his own designers is counterintuitive: just do less, lean on AI for the mechanical parts of the job, and spend the time saved on the things humans still do better, understanding what users actually need and forming a genuine point of view, rather than just producing more screens faster. Via Lenny's Newsletter.
Now, over to startups and venture.
The unicorn factory is running hotter than ever. Crunchbase data shows the world minted one hundred and ninety five new unicorns in just the first half of twenty twenty six, already surpassing the entirety of last year, with robotics and AI leading the charge and the United States and China dominating the totals between them. Via TLDR, by way of The VC Corner's own weekly roundup.
In Europe, the round sizes are getting harder to ignore. Index Ventures is reportedly in talks to lead a five hundred million dollar round for a brand new AI lab founded by a former DeepMind researcher, while Spanish model-compression startup Multiverse Computing is said to be chasing a two billion euro valuation on technology that claims to shrink large AI models by up to ninety five percent with barely any loss in accuracy, a pitch that has already won over customers including Bosch and the Bank of Canada. Closer to home for builders, AI coding assistant Lovable closed a four hundred million dollar round at a valuation of thirteen point three billion dollars, continuing one of the fastest climbs in the sector this year. Via The VC Corner.
And Nvidia is trying something genuinely new with its balance sheet. The company has signed financing agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, aiming to pull in more than five hundred billion dollars from outside investors to fund AI data centres, effectively pitching raw compute as a durable, resaleable financial asset in its own right. The catch, critics note, is that these are non-binding agreements rather than signed cheques, and Nvidia's own participation in deals already exceeds its trailing cash flow, which raises real questions about customer concentration and what these chips would actually be worth if a buyer walked away. Via The VC Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
CSIS's weekly numbers round-up is worth lingering on this week. The United States currently maintains roughly six thousand eight hundred Russia and Ukraine related sanctions designations, and nearly all of them were put in place before January twenty twenty five, after which new designation activity essentially flatlined while Washington pursued negotiations with Moscow, a pattern worth watching if Congress moves to codify those sanctions into law. Meanwhile, the bilateral goods trade deficit between the United States and China fell from two hundred and ninety seven billion dollars in twenty twenty four to two hundred and two point seven billion dollars in twenty twenty five, though the researchers caution that the improvement reflects falling American exports as much as falling imports, which rather undercuts any straightforward reading of it as a policy win. Via CSIS.
And a grimmer number from the same source: Sudan is estimated to have produced seventy four point six tons of gold in twenty twenty five, placing it among the world's top twenty producers, and that gold revenue is now a key funding line for every side of the country's civil war, a reminder that some of the most consequential resource flows in global conflicts barely make the headlines. Via CSIS.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, one idea worth stealing today.
Community strategist and DO Lectures collaborator Sabine has a lovely, low-tech idea worth borrowing for anyone trying to build a community around content rather than just broadcast it. The format is a listening club, thirty people gather to listen to a single show together for an hour, in total silence, and anyone who breaks that silence has to buy drinks for the whole group afterwards. It is a tiny bit of social stakes turning a passive listening habit into a genuinely shared, memorable event, and it costs almost nothing to run. Via The DO Lectures.
A second idea worth stealing, this one about the unglamorous side of building an audience. Newsletter growth writer Chenell Basilio borrowed a scene from the television show The Bear, where a chaotic sandwich cook is sent to a fine-dining kitchen and given a single task for his entire first week: polishing forks. The point, once he finally gets it, is that customers do not just experience the headline product, they experience every small unattended moment around it, the signup page, the welcome email, the follow-up nobody thought to check. Her advice for anyone running a newsletter, a community or a product: treat those overlooked moments, not just the big weekly send, as part of what you are actually building. Via Growth In Reverse.
And finally, one interesting thing.
Economist and blogger Tyler Cowen flagged a small but telling story out of Washington DC this week. Metro bus drivers there were recently told to start verbally announcing the two dollar twenty five cent fare to every passenger who boards, a policy meant to cut down on the roughly seventy percent of riders who do not pay. Several drivers are quietly ignoring the instruction anyway, telling reporters that calling out the price to strangers on a bus makes them feel more likely to be harassed or even assaulted over it than if the fare simply went unmentioned. It is a small, human illustration of what economists call sticky prices, the idea that the friction and social cost of actually stating a price out loud can matter just as much as the price itself.
That is your six sections for today. Thank you for listening to Byte-sized, and I will be back with the next episode soon. Take care.

item.title: Byte-sized — Week in review, 16 August
item.description:
Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized, week of the tenth to the sixteenth of August. This is the week in review, so rather than a fresh run through the daily news, think of this as the six stories from each section that still mattered by the time Sunday rolled around. Same six sections as always: Japan and Asia-Pacific, AI and tech, startups and venture, policy and geopolitics, community, events and marketing, and one interesting thing to close things out. Let's get into it.
Japan and Asia-Pacific this week was a story of quiet domestic resilience running alongside mounting pressure from China across the wider region.
First up, Fukuoka's preparedness moment. Fukuoka is formally pushing to become one of Japan's official backup capital cities, a status created by new national legislation designed to keep government functions running if a major disaster strikes Tokyo. The push landed just days after a University of Tokyo seismologist warned locals that an unruptured section of the nearby Kego fault zone should be treated as a serious, live risk rather than a distant one, which gives the backup capital bid a rather pointed local backdrop. In the same week, the wider Kyushu and Okinawa region's population slipped below fourteen million for the first time on record, even as its foreign resident numbers kept climbing, a demographic split that's becoming familiar across regional Japan. And Sony and TSMC pressed ahead with a roughly seven hundred and forty seven billion yen joint sensor plant in Kumamoto, a reminder that the chip investment boom in Kyushu hasn't slowed even as the local population does. Via Fukuoka Now.
Next, a case for deeper US-Japan collaboration on culture, not just chips or defence. A new paper from the CSIS Japan Chair argues that Japan and the United States should combine their complementary strengths, Japan's globally competitive intellectual property and America's dominant digital platforms, to expand their reach across the international creative and entertainment industries. The paper points out that creative industries are already a meaningful source of American economic growth and export earnings, and that Japan is now treating its own creative sector as a strategic pillar of long-term competitiveness, which makes the two countries unusually well matched. The authors frame this as more than a commercial opportunity: as competition for global audiences intensifies, closer collaboration on content could help both countries shape the wider information environment in a positive direction, while deepening people to people ties across the Indo-Pacific over the long term. Via CSIS.
Then, a small diplomatic needle. Tokyo lodged a formal complaint after Vladimir Putin made his first ever visit to the Kuril Islands, a chain the Soviets seized from Japan at the end of the Second World War and which Tokyo still partly claims, a dispute that is one reason the two countries never signed a formal postwar peace treaty. The timing looks pointed: the trip came just after Japan's government published a new defence white paper warning about growing cooperation between Russia, China and North Korea, making the visit read as a deliberate jab timed to Tokyo's own security messaging. Via International Intrigue.
And finally, a warning that the region's biggest security story isn't really about the sea at all. A detailed CSIS analysis lays out how China is squeezing the Philippines through eight interlocking levers, from disinformation and elite capture to cyber operations and coast guard coercion, arguing that the headline-grabbing standoffs in the South China Sea are really just the tip of a much broader campaign. The report notes that Filipino public opinion still favours Washington over Beijing by a wide margin, but warns that this advantage could prove more fragile than it looks from Washington if recent policy missteps and energy shocks keep chipping away at it. And the author says this is a playbook China is already extending elsewhere in the region, pointing to a recent Chinese ballistic missile test fired into the Pacific and intensified pressure on both Japan and New Zealand in just the past few weeks, which makes the Philippines less an isolated dispute and more an early warning for everyone else nearby. Via CSIS.
Now, over to AI and tech, where the headlines this week were about how fast frontier models are moving, and who is quietly paying for the compute behind them.
xAI released Grok four point six, a model tuned for long running agents, coding and knowledge work, and it immediately jumped into the top tier of the field. The new model ties GPT five point six Sol Max for third place on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, overtaking Kimi K3 in the process, while undercutting GPT five point six sharply on price, at two dollars per million input tokens and six dollars per million output tokens, less than half of what OpenAI charges in standard mode. It's another sign that the gap at the very top of the leaderboard keeps narrowing, even as the price war underneath it keeps intensifying. Via TLDR.
Anthropic announced it will start quietly embedding an invisible watermark into text generated by Claude, though it hasn't disclosed exactly how the method works. Researchers who have looked into it believe the marker lives in a subtle statistical bias in word choice, one robust enough to survive ordinary copying and pasting, though simple countermeasures like paraphrasing or a full rewrite could likely strip it back out again. Via TLDR.
And Nvidia made a bold attempt to turn its chips into a new kind of financial asset. The company unveiled financing platforms built with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, aiming to raise more than five hundred billion dollars from outside investors to fund AI data centres, with chief executive Jensen Huang pitching compute itself as a durable, resaleable, investable asset class. Sceptics were quick to point out that these are non-binding agreements rather than signed deals, and that the entire pitch rests on unproven resale value, since Nvidia's own evidence for durability, rising rental rates on older chips, really only proves current earnings, not what the hardware would actually fetch if a customer walked away. Via TLDR.
And away from the frontier labs, a quieter story about who is actually training the robots of the future. Tens of thousands of workers in India are being recruited to film themselves doing ordinary, mundane tasks in first person, footage that is then fed into AI systems designed to teach robots how to physically interact with the world. It's a reminder that even as the headlines focus on chatbots and coding agents, the harder unsolved problem in robotics is simply a shortage of real footage of humans doing everyday things, because until very recently nobody thought that footage was worth collecting at all. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture, where the story of the week was scale: more new unicorns in six months than in the whole of last year, and mega rounds chasing whoever looks like the next frontier lab.
The world minted one hundred and ninety five new unicorns in the first half of twenty twenty six alone, according to Crunchbase data, already surpassing the entire total for twenty twenty five, with robotics and AI leading the surge. China's DeepSeek and Seychelles based crypto exchange OKX both crossed major valuation milestones during the period, and the United States and China dominated overall, with fast follow funding rounds pushing valuations up rapidly across both AI and semiconductor startups. Via TLDR.
In Europe, Index Ventures is reportedly in talks to lead a five hundred million dollar round for a brand new AI lab founded by a former DeepMind researcher, one of several outsized raises reported this week. In the same stretch, Spanish AI model compression startup Multiverse Computing was said to be pushing for a two billion euro valuation on the back of technology that claims to shrink large AI models by up to ninety five percent with little loss in accuracy, a pitch that's already landed it more than a hundred customers including Bosch and the Bank of Canada. Drone maker Uforce, meanwhile, was reportedly targeting a valuation upwards of four billion dollars in its next round, and coding assistant Lovable closed a four hundred million dollar round backed partly by the European Union's own Scaleup fund, a deal that raised eyebrows given the fund was originally pitched as being for defence, space and quantum technology rather than a consumer coding tool. Via Sifted.
And in China, Moonshot, the maker of the Kimi K3 model, announced a three and a half billion dollar raise at a thirty five billion dollar valuation, with a Hong Kong listing reportedly under consideration. The timing raised eyebrows well beyond its own investors, since the round landed squarely in the middle of a US Treasury investigation into intellectual property theft allegations against Chinese open model makers, making it an unusually large vote of confidence delivered mid-scandal. It capped a week in which AI kept pushing into new corners of everyday life across Asia too, with reports of AI reaching into drug discovery, hospital records and even autonomous payments, a reminder that the contest between open and closed models is playing out well beyond the leaderboards. Via Speeda Uzabase.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics, where the week's conversation circled oil markets, an escalating trade fight, and Europe's newest AI rulebook starting to bite.
BlackRock's latest geopolitical risk dashboard, compiled with a former US national security advisor and two former central bankers, flagged four themes worth watching for the rest of the year: energy markets staying vulnerable to renewed price spikes even without outright shortages, an escalating trade fight between Europe and China over cheap Chinese exports, continued US economic and diplomatic pressure on Latin American governments it considers adversarial, and no meaningful US-China cooperation on frontier AI beyond a narrow new dialogue focused purely on safety practices. The single most striking number in the report: China's trade surplus with the European Union has now overtaken its surplus with the United States for the first time in thirty years, and Germany, once China's second largest buyer, has slipped all the way down to ninth, a shift that helps explain why Brussels and Beijing keep trading tit for tat probes, from electric vehicles to cognac to pork. Via International Intrigue.
Closer to the ground, the European Union's AI Act is starting to reshape how an entire consumer facing industry talks to its customers. The Act's requirements for clear labelling of AI generated content and transparency whenever a customer is interacting with an AI system are now filtering into travel, forcing airlines, hotels and booking platforms to rethink how they disclose AI use at the point of booking, one of the clearest early examples yet of the Act's transparency rules landing on an everyday consumer sector rather than staying confined to enterprise software. It lands the same week separate industry research found travellers broadly want AI to personalise their trips, but draw a hard line at unchecked autonomy, wanting to stay firmly in control of the final decision. Via PhocusWire.
And a quieter but arguably bigger story: economists are now arguing humanity has likely dropped below replacement level fertility for the first time in recorded history, a milestone that survived even wars and pandemics. A new paper highlighted on Marginal Revolution examined two hundred and thirty six countries going back to 1950 and found the decline is concentrated among poorer, less educated women in low and middle income countries rather than wealthy ones, with no single global driver behind it, and not one of two hundred and nineteen country-specific trends the researchers identified is currently levelling off. That leads the authors to a blunt conjecture: modernity itself makes a third child expensive and childlessness cheap, and because children come in whole numbers, it takes very little economic change to knock a country's fertility rate down and nothing much in a modern economy to push it back up again, which is why the paper closes on slow growth as the main long run economic consequence. Via Marginal Revolution.
Now, over to community, events and marketing, two ideas worth stealing this week, both about the harder, less glamorous side of bringing people together.
One idea worth stealing: treat group conflict as a skill, not a crisis to be avoided. Facilitator Priya Parker announced her second book, The Art of Fighting, arguing that most existing conflict advice is built for pairs, spouses, business partners, and leaves groups, teams, communities, families, with almost no real tools beyond pretending everything is fine one day and reaching for a lawsuit the next. She traces the idea back to 2020, when the same skills she'd built for designing joyful gatherings turned out to be exactly what clients needed most once the pandemic and a wave of institutional reckonings pushed group tension out into the open. Her practical suggestion for anyone running a team or a community: build small, deliberate rituals for surfacing tension early, the same kind of intentional design she brought to gatherings in her first book, rather than waiting for a full blow-up before anyone addresses it. Via Priya Parker.
The second idea worth stealing: you can build real community even in spaces you don't own. Community strategist Shyaamal Tripathi shared hard-won lessons from building community inside Discord servers, forums and events he did not control himself, drawing on experience from a student hackathon, a Web3 project and an enterprise software company. His core takeaway for anyone trying to grow a following on someone else's platform: you earn a seat at the table by consistently adding value on other people's turf first, long before you ever ask for anything back, since nobody owes a newcomer trust just because they showed up with something to promote. Via Community Inc.
And finally, one interesting thing to close out the week.
Does animal welfare follow the same curve as air pollution once did? A Works in Progress essay asks whether farm animal suffering will eventually shrink the way pollution and deforestation did as countries grew richer, the pattern economists call a Kuznets curve, named for the economist who first noticed inequality rises then falls as nations industrialise. The uncomfortable finding: some wealthy nations, Germany among them, are genuinely eating a fifth less meat than they used to, but the meat they do eat has shifted heavily from beef towards chicken and farmed fish, so per person they now cause roughly twice as many animals to suffer as they did forty years ago, not fewer, since a single serving of chicken implies vastly more days of a suffering animal's life than the same serving of beef. It's a reminder that getting richer doesn't automatically bend every curve the way it eventually bent the smog over London.
That's your week, all six sections, sorted. Thank you for listening to Byte-sized, and I'll be back with the next episode soon. Take care.

item.title: Byte-sized — Saturday, 15 August
item.description:
Hello, it's Saturday the fifteenth of August, and this is Byte-sized, your six-part rundown of today's newsletters, in about ten to fifteen minutes.
Japan and Asia-Pacific first.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies has a new paper from Makoto Tsujiguchi arguing that Japan's creative industries are becoming a strategic pillar of its economic policy. The idea is straightforward: pair Japan's globally competitive intellectual property with America's dominant digital platforms, and the two countries can expand their reach across the Indo-Pacific, deepen digital trade, and compete harder for global audiences against Korean and Chinese content industries, all while shaping the information environment and deepening people-to-people ties along the way. It is as much a soft-power argument as an economic one: culture as a lever for the alliance, not just entertainment for its own sake. Via CSIS Japan Chair.
Staying regional, CSIS also published its monthly Pac-Tech Pulse, tracking technology policy across the Indo-Pacific, and Japan features prominently. Tokyo has released a second Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan, aimed at accelerating the rollout of smart technologies while tightening up cybersecurity and regulatory oversight. It lands alongside a wave of regional moves: Australia has stood up a new AI framework, an Office of AI, and rules forcing data centres to underwrite the power and water they consume; South Korea is pushing "physical AI" strategies for robotics, ports and manufacturing; Thailand has tightened its screening of data centre investment; and Vietnam has published its first official list of high-risk AI systems. The throughline is that Asia-Pacific governments are moving from AI enthusiasm to AI governance, all at once, and Japan is positioning itself firmly on the regulatory end of that spectrum. Via CSIS Pac-Tech Pulse.
Reuters, picked up in CSIS's Nuclear Policy News briefing, explains why North Korea has been ramping up criticism of Japan. Pyongyang has stepped up its rhetoric against Japan's military buildup and its security cooperation with the United States and South Korea, framing all three as a threat to regional stability. It's a reminder that Japan's own defence posture is increasingly part of the story in Northeast Asian tension, not just a bystander to it. Via CSIS Nuclear Policy News.
And CSIS's Southeast Asia programme turned its podcast to Cambodia's scam centre ecosystem this week, with reporter Shibani Mahtani discussing how the industry has evolved and why its implications now reach well beyond Cambodia's own borders, into the wider region's trafficking and fraud networks. Via CSIS Southeast Asia Radio.
Now, over to AI and tech.
The headline model release this week was Grok four point six from SpaceXAI, which the company says now matches GPT five point six Sol on the main industry benchmark and overtakes China's Kimi K3, with particular strength in long-running coding and agent tasks. It's notably cheaper too, priced at two dollars per million input tokens and six dollars per million output tokens, well under half of what GPT five point six costs to run in standard mode. Via TLDR.
Google, meanwhile, rolled out Gemini three point seven Flash just three weeks after its predecessor, an unusually fast turnaround the company puts down to developer feedback, alongside a temporary fifty percent price cut aimed squarely at coding and agent workloads. OpenAI answered with a preview of an "Ultrafast" mode for GPT five point six Sol, capable of fourteen times its standard processing speed. The frontier labs are now racing each other on speed and price as much as raw intelligence. Via TLDR.
The bigger financial story, though, is Anthropic. Investors are now pricing a potential initial public offering at over two trillion dollars, which would make it the largest listing in history, on the back of projected annualised revenue of up to one hundred and twenty billion dollars by the end of the year. On the product side, the company also upgraded Claude in Chrome this week, so the browser side panel now runs a full Cowork session that saves to your account and picks up on desktop or mobile. It's a striking combination for a company that barely existed as a household name three years ago, and it says a lot about how much capital is still flowing into frontier AI despite the wobbles elsewhere in the sector. Via TLDR.
On the enterprise side, IBM is launching a dedicated OpenAI consulting practice, with plans to certify tens of thousands of consultants and jointly build AI offerings for finance, government, telecoms and retail. It lands in the same week Cisco reported its AI infrastructure orders have hit nine point three billion dollars for the year, and it's the clearest sign yet that OpenAI is chasing the same enterprise services market that Anthropic, Cisco and the big consultancies are already fighting over. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Swedish vibe-coding platform Lovable has closed a four hundred million dollar Series C, taking its valuation to thirteen point three billion dollars, with the round co-led by the EU's new Scaleup Europe Fund alongside Menlo Ventures, and the company is reportedly on track for a revenue run rate approaching six hundred million dollars by the end of this month. It's a slightly awkward fit for a fund meant to back European tech sovereignty in areas like defence and quantum, and it's raised a few eyebrows in Sifted's own newsroom, but it underlines just how much capital is chasing the application layer of AI right now. Via Sifted and TLDR.
Index Ventures is reportedly in talks to lead a five hundred million dollar round for a new AI lab founded by an ex-DeepMind researcher, focused on world models, the technology that lets AI systems simulate and reason about physical environments rather than just text. If it closes, it would be one of the largest seed-stage AI bets of the year, and it lands in the same week that three departing partners from London's LocalGlobe were reported to be exploring a spin-out fund of their own, part of a broader reshuffle running through European venture right now. Via Sifted.
And Databricks has acquired Electric, a startup whose technology lets AI agents keep a fast, local copy of a database in sync with a central one. The team is joining Databricks' Neon unit to build infrastructure specifically for agentic applications, another sign that the plumbing underneath AI agents, not just the models themselves, is becoming its own competitive battleground. Via TLDR.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
CSIS's Foreign Affairs piece this week, from Caitlin Welsh and Brian Hart, digs into what they call China's Hunger Games: Beijing's habit of using access to its enormous agricultural import market as geopolitical leverage, from suspending American soybean purchases during the tariff fight, to cutting off Canadian canola over EV tariffs, to briefly halting Japanese seafood and sake imports last year over Taiwan tensions. The twist is that this leverage cuts both ways. China imports over two hundred billion dollars of food a year and depends on foreign suppliers for the vast majority of its soybeans, which is exactly why Beijing is now racing to build up its own agricultural biotechnology, so it can eventually wield exports as a weapon too, not just imports. Via CSIS.
And in Europe, Bloomberg reports that Sweden, one of the continent's most committed disarmament voices, is quietly rethinking its historic rejection of nuclear-armed alliances as the perceived threat from Russia grows. It's a small but telling data point in a broader pattern of traditionally neutral or dovish states hardening their security posture, and it landed the same day NATO jets shot down a drone that had entered Latvian airspace, which Latvia's military blamed on Russian electromagnetic warfare. Via CSIS Nuclear Policy News.
Further south, Saudi Arabia and thirteen other countries have confirmed a new maritime defence coalition to protect shipping through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, with more members expected to join. The Financial Times frames it alongside Pakistan's own more assertive turn, including a fresh defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, as part of a wider reshuffling of Middle Eastern and South Asian security alliances that's easy to miss amid the AI headlines but matters just as much for anyone tracking where the next flashpoints sit. Via CSIS Nuclear Policy News.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Priya Parker, best known for The Art of Gathering, is following it up with a new book called The Art of Fighting, about how groups stay together through real conflict rather than falling apart into ghosting, walkouts and lawsuits. Her practical takeaway is that most conflict advice out there is written for pairs, couples, business partners, but groups need their own rituals and infrastructure for handling tension, the same kind of deliberate design she's long argued goes into a good gathering. It's worth stealing for anyone running a team, a community or a family through a rough patch, whether that's a seating chart fight or a group chat that's quietly imploding. Via Priya Parker's newsletter.
And Marketing Brew flagged what it's calling the rise of the "brand puppet," with skincare brand CeraVe among those leaning into cartoonish, personality-driven characters in their social content rather than straight product messaging, as a way to cut through an increasingly noisy feed. The idea worth stealing: a recurring character can carry a brand's voice further, and feel less like an ad, than another polished product post ever will. Via Marketing Brew.
And finally, one interesting thing.
Ahead of Delhi's badminton world championships, the city has been hiring people for a genuinely strange job: professional langur-monkey impersonators. The screech of a langur is apparently the only reliable way to scare off the rhesus macaques that roam the city stealing food and causing chaos, so a handful of Indians have turned mimicking a much larger, more intimidating monkey into a paid pest-control gig, protecting the tournament venues one shriek at a time. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's Byte-sized for Saturday. Have a good weekend, and I'll be back tomorrow with the week in review.

item.title: Byte-sized — Friday, 14 August
item.description:
# Byte-sized — Thursday, 14 August
Good morning. It's Friday the fourteenth of August, and this is Byte-sized, your daily digest of newsletters, in six parts. Let's get into it.
Japan and Asia-Pacific first.
Tokyo has lodged a formal protest after Vladimir Putin paid his first-ever visit to the Kuril Islands, the chain seized by the Soviets after the Second World War but still partly claimed by Japan. Russian state media confirmed Putin visited Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, this week. The timing is pointed: Japan's prime minister, Takaichi, recently released a new defence white paper warning about growing cooperation between Russia, China and North Korea, so a high-profile trip to the fortified islands reads as a deliberate jab at Tokyo. It also underlines a point security commentators keep making, that Japan's defence posture still rests on an uneasy contradiction: a nation devoutly opposed to nuclear weapons that continues to shelter under America's nuclear umbrella. Via CSIS and International Intrigue.
Next, Japan has released the second version of its national Artificial Intelligence Basic Plan, aiming to speed up the rollout of smart technology to tackle national challenges while tightening up regulation and cybersecurity safeguards. It lands as part of a much bigger wave of AI policy-making breaking out across the region. Australia has stood up a new Office of AI and promised to protect creative works from being scraped for training data. China has published action plans on AI cooperation and on AI ethics governance. South Korea is pushing "physical AI" strategies for robotics, ports and manufacturing. Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Pakistan have all published their own frameworks in the past month. The upshot: Indo-Pacific governments are no longer waiting on Washington or Brussels to set the rules for AI, they're writing their own. Via CSIS's Pac-Tech Pulse newsletter.
And in Southeast Asia, CSIS's Greg and Elina sat down with journalist Shibani Mahtani to unpack the evolving scam centre ecosystem in Cambodia, which has grown from a localised criminal enterprise into a regional problem with implications well beyond its borders. The conversation is a reminder that the region's digital economy has a dark underside that governments are still struggling to contain. Via CSIS Southeast Asia Radio.
Now, over to AI and tech.
SpaceX's AI division has released Grok four point six, a model tuned for long-running agents, coding and knowledge work. It now matches OpenAI's GPT five point six Sol on independent benchmarks while undercutting it on price by around sixty percent, and it's already overtaken Kimi K3 for third place on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard. It's the latest sign that frontier AI pricing is becoming as competitive a battleground as raw capability. Via TLDR and This Week in Startups.
Anthropic is reportedly in early talks to acquire the Israeli startup Decart for around six billion dollars, a deal that would bring Decart's chip optimisation technology in-house. If it goes ahead, it would be one of Anthropic's largest acquisitions to date and points to how seriously the big AI labs are taking the cost of compute. Separately, Anthropic confirmed it will begin embedding invisible watermarks in text and images generated by Claude, bringing it in line with the European Union's AI Act code of practice. The text watermark survives copying and light editing, though the company admits detection can fail on short or heavily rewritten snippets. Via TLDR Design and CTech.
And Databricks has raised five billion dollars at a valuation of one hundred and ninety billion dollars, cementing its place as one of the most valuable private companies in AI infrastructure. The raise lands the same week Databricks confirmed it's acquiring Electric, a startup whose lightweight, in-browser version of Postgres lets AI agents keep fast local databases that sync back to a central source of truth. Together the moves show Databricks racing to own the plumbing that agentic AI will run on. Via TLDR IT.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Sifted reports that Index Ventures is in talks to lead a five hundred million dollar round for a new AI lab founded by a former DeepMind researcher, focused on so-called world models, AI systems designed to simulate and reason about physical environments rather than just text. It would be one of the largest seed-stage AI bets of the year if it closes. Via Sifted.
OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings, which buys traditional businesses and rebuilds them around AI, has raised two billion dollars at a twelve billion dollar valuation from SoftBank, D1 Capital Partners and Altimeter. It's a striking bet that the fastest way to monetise AI isn't building new software companies, but retrofitting old ones. Via This Week in Startups.
And in Europe, two rounds worth watching: the vibe-coding platform Lovable closed a four hundred million dollar Series C backed by the European Union's own Scaleup Fund, while Portuguese drone maker Uforce is said to be targeting a valuation north of four billion dollars in its next raise. Between them they capture the twin themes of the moment, AI-native software and defence-adjacent hardware, both pulling in serious European capital. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, published its latest geopolitical risk dashboard this week, and two calls stand out. First, on trade: the dashboard flags the European Union's dispute with China over industrial overcapacity as the year's likely flashpoint. China's manufacturing surplus has now reached roughly two percent of global GDP, its trade surplus with the EU has overtaken its surplus with the United States for the first time in three decades, and Beijing has been retaliating selectively against European exports, from French cognac to Spanish pork, whenever Brussels moves on electric vehicle tariffs. With Washington and Brussels not exactly aligned right now, Europe may be facing this one largely alone. Second, on AI: BlackRock doesn't expect meaningful US-China cooperation on frontier AI any time soon, but notes a narrow opening has appeared. May's Trump-Xi summit produced a new bilateral dialogue on AI "best practices," with a first working round due next month, ahead of a planned reciprocal Xi visit to the US. The goal isn't friendship, it's avoiding a repeat of Cold War-style nuclear near misses, this time with AI systems instead of warheads. Via International Intrigue.
Separately, Zhu Rongji, China's former premier and the hard-charging technocrat who drove the country's entry into the World Trade Organization, has died at ninety-seven. His legacy splits sharply depending on who you ask: the state-firm workers who lost jobs under his efficiency drives, the hundreds of millions who rode China's post-WTO boom into the middle class, and the workers abroad who lost out to the China shock that followed. It's a reminder of how consequential, and how contested, that period of Chinese economic opening still is. Via International Intrigue.
And a live example of why supply chains keep showing up on the geopolitical risk radar: a cyberattack this week disrupted eight warehouses run by the logistics giant Ceva, delaying or cancelling orders for retailers across Europe, including hardware customers of the online retailer Bol and gaming customers of Valve. Attackers reportedly accessed order-processing systems containing names, addresses and purchase details. It's a small story on its own, but it's the kind of quietly cascading disruption that boardrooms increasingly have to plan around, alongside tariffs and export controls, when they think about resilience. Via TLDR.
Now, over to community, events and marketing. One idea worth stealing from each.
From the Community Inc newsletter: most community-building advice assumes you already own a platform, a forum, a Discord, an events calendar. Writer Shyaamal Tripathi makes the case for building trust in spaces you don't control instead, drawing on his experience growing communities inside other people's Discord servers, hackathons and open-source projects. The practical takeaway: show up consistently, add value without asking for credit, and let the trust you build outlast any single platform. Via Community Inc.
From SEO writer Zyppy Signal, on how Google actually judges content quality: buried in a leaked Google ranking document is a signal called "content effort," estimated by a large language model for every page it crawls. The point isn't how long something took to make, it's whether the finished page shows visible evidence of real work, original testing, first-hand opinions, unique photography, curated judgment, rather than being a repackaging of what's already on the internet. For anyone publishing anything, physical or digital, the one-line lesson is: make the effort visible, don't just make it. Via Zyppy Signal.
And now, one interesting thing to close on.
Thrift stores are having a moment again, and the internet has decided secondhand shopping is content. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published a report this year marvelling at how many millennials and Gen Z-ers now flock to thrift shops, and resale platform ThredUp reckons the worldwide secondhand clothing market will hit nearly four hundred billion dollars within four years. Writer Jason Boog traces the through-line back to a New York Sun article from nineteen-oh-two, describing the same cast of characters haunting a Brooklyn Salvation Army store: bargain hunters, canny resellers, and one gum-chewing teenager after a good pair of shoes for the dance. More than a century on, her spiritual heirs are the same age, filming "thrift with me" videos that have racked up millions of posts on TikTok. Some things, it turns out, really don't change. Via Why Is This Interesting.
That's your six for today. Thanks for listening, and I'll see you tomorrow.
---

Hello, and welcome to Byte-sized for Thursday, the thirteenth of August. Six sections today, starting with Japan and Asia-Pacific.
Sony and Taiwan's TSMC are in talks to build a joint image sensor plant in Kumamoto, in southern Japan, in a deal reportedly worth six point four billion dollars. The investment adds to Kumamoto's rapid transformation into one of the most important chip manufacturing hubs in Asia, building on TSMC's earlier decision to put fabrication plants there. For Japan, it's another marker of how the country has positioned itself as the trusted manufacturing partner of choice as global chipmakers diversify away from single points of failure elsewhere in the region. Via TLDR.
North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast this week, days ahead of major joint military exercises between South Korea and the United States that Pyongyang has long condemned. Both South Korean and Japanese authorities confirmed the launch. It's a familiar pattern of North Korean signalling before allied drills, but it lands against a wider regional backdrop of persistent worry about Beijing's own military build-up, from expanding submarine fleets to a nuclear stockpile that keeps growing. Via CSIS.
Chinese AI chip designer Moore Threads has filed for a Hong Kong stock listing to raise capital for global research and development. The company, founded by former Nvidia executives, is positioning itself alongside Huawei and Cambricon to capture China's domestic AI data centre hardware market while Nvidia faces continued American export restrictions. It's a reminder that even as leading Chinese AI labs still lean heavily on Nvidia chips to train their frontier models, the domestic alternative stack is being built out with real capital behind it. Via TLDR.
Microsoft is also expanding its footprint in the region, negotiating with TSMC to reserve manufacturing capacity for more than three hundred thousand of its next-generation Maia AI accelerator chips. It's another sign of how central Taiwanese foundries remain to the entire AI buildout, whatever the political tension hanging over the island. Via TLDR.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Nvidia is trying to turn AI computing power into Wall Street's next asset class. The company announced financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR, aiming to raise more than five hundred billion dollars in outside capital to build so-called AI factories, the data centres that train and run AI models. Chief executive Jensen Huang is pitching this compute capacity as a durable, reusable investment, but critics point out these are non-binding agreements rather than signed deals, and the entire pitch rests on what the hardware would actually be worth if a paying customer walked away. Via TLDR.
There's been a wave of leadership change at the top of the industry this week. OpenAI's long-serving chief operating officer, Brad Lightcap, is leaving to start a new venture, the latest in a run of senior departures as the company prepares for its stock market listing. Over at Google, Koray Kavukcuoglu has been promoted to head Google DeepMind, taking charge of Gemini's development as the company chases OpenAI and Anthropic, just as Google announced that the Gemini app has passed one billion monthly active users. Via TLDR.
Anthropic says it will start embedding an invisible watermark into text generated by Claude, though it hasn't disclosed exactly how. Security researchers reckon it works as a subtle statistical bias in word choice, which should survive ordinary copying and pasting, though determined attackers could likely strip it out by rewriting or regenerating the text. It's a small but telling move in the industry's slow build toward being able to tell human and machine writing apart, at exactly the point when that distinction is getting harder to make. Via TLDR.
Coding tool Cursor looks set to expand beyond writing code and into reviewing it too. The company appears to be preparing a wider launch of a platform called Cursor Review, which syncs with repositories pulled in from GitHub and runs an automated pull request pipeline that flags when a human's judgement is needed, letting people and AI agents work through open pull requests together. It's part of a broader shift in how coding tools are positioning themselves, not just as autocomplete, but as a genuine second pair of eyes on a codebase. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture.
More companies became unicorns in the first half of this year than in the whole of last year combined. A hundred and ninety five companies crossed the billion dollar valuation mark in the first six months of twenty twenty six, according to Crunchbase data, with robotics and AI leading the surge. China's DeepSeek and Seychelles-based crypto exchange OKX were among the standouts, reaching fifty billion and twenty five billion dollars respectively, with the United States and China dominating overall. Via TLDR.
Robotics startups alone have raised twenty three billion dollars so far this year, underlining just how much investor appetite has shifted toward physical AI and automation, on top of the software wave that came before it. Via TLDR.
In Europe, a trio of former LocalGlobe investors are reportedly in early talks to raise a new venture fund, while Nick Blair, the youngest son of former UK prime minister Tony Blair, is seeking two hundred million dollars for a new defence technology startup. Both point to the same trend: European venture capital is increasingly chasing two of its hottest categories right now, experienced operators striking out on their own, and defence technology drawing serious money as the continent rearms. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has resurfaced after months out of public view, ending speculation that he was gravely injured or even dead following this year's war with Israel and the United States. Almost immediately afterwards, decrees issued in his name filled six of the most powerful military posts left vacant by that war, installing hardline loyalists across the Revolutionary Guard, the regular armed forces, and the Basij militia that enforces internal repression. Analysts at International Intrigue read the appointments as a clear signal: Iran's surviving hardliners are consolidating control at home and showing zero interest in external compromise, whatever the truth about Mojtaba's health. Via International Intrigue.
Pakistan's foreign minister has described a new defence pact his country signed with Saudi Arabia and Turkey as purely defensive and open to other nations in the region. The agreement adds another layer to the web of Middle Eastern security arrangements being renegotiated in the aftermath of the Iran war, as regional powers hedge against future instability without committing fully to any single bloc. Via CSIS.
Back in Washington, the general running the Golden Dome missile defence programme has warned it is in real trouble, after the White House opted to seek most of its twenty twenty seven funding through a contested budget manoeuvre rather than a straightforward appropriation from Congress. Without reliable funding, he warned bluntly, there is no Golden Dome. It's a reminder that even flagship defence programmes rest on unglamorous questions of budget process as much as on technology. Via CSIS.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing: tell your best customer stories out loud, not just in writing. For the third year running, the dating app Hinge is reviving its "No Ordinary Love" campaign, which tells real stories of couples who met on the platform, but this year it's leaning hard into audio, including its first full audiobook, aimed at reaching Gen Z daters who increasingly prefer to listen rather than read. The brand's marketing chief says audio lets them tell deeper, more emotional stories than a written format allows. If your best customer stories are still sitting in a written case study, it might be worth asking whether they'd land harder read aloud. Via Marketing Brew.
One idea worth stealing: keep the ordinary rituals going, especially when things are hard. Sifted spoke to founders and employees at Ukrainian startups about how they keep team morale alive under the constant strain of war, and the answers were strikingly ordinary: quiz nights, picnics, flexible time off after a bad night of attacks, and a lot of explicit permission to say when things aren't okay. One founder said going on holiday abroad actually made him feel worse, because he lost the sense of control that comes from being with his team. It's a reminder that under real pressure, the basics of team culture matter more, not less. Via Sifted.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Researchers studying more than a decade of Russian survey data found something uncomfortable: life satisfaction among ordinary Russians rose significantly after the twenty twenty two invasion of Ukraine, even after accounting for people's material circumstances. The gains were largest among ethnic Russians and in military-industrial regions, smaller in Moscow and St Petersburg, and sharply lower near the front line, a pattern the researchers say is hard to explain away as people simply telling pollsters what the regime wants to hear. By twenty twenty four, though, more people were refusing to answer the survey at all, which the authors suspect means the picture is quietly getting harder to read. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's Byte-sized for Thursday the thirteenth of August. See you tomorrow.
